<reason>Both sides built genuinely strong, well-matched cases, but A's central move — that CON's "remediation on notice, penalties for refusal" alternative is functionally a fine mechanism with different labels — was raised early (A2.1), pressed hard in the pressure round (A3.1), and never fully dislodged. B's best material (compliance theater, small-provider withdrawal, circularity) was substantively answered: theater is defeated once the trigger is actual repeated failure rather than a paperwork audit; small-provider harm was reframed as evidence the bar is already too low or as a redesign question rather than a reason to abandon fines; circularity was answered by earmarking remedial funds. B's strongest surviving point — that the literal motion text implies strict liability on outcomes, punishing good-faith remediators — is a fair textual observation, but A's notice-and-correction reading was present from the opening (A1.2), not smuggled in late, and tracks ordinary regulatory analogues (OSHA, tax abatement) that B never seriously rebutted. By the closing, A's framing that "the only disagreement left is rhetorical" went largely unanswered in substance; B reasserted the asymmetry but didn't show why it should decide the vote. Both sides suffered one clipped turn, a wash on execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over whether CON's "remediation on notice, penalties for refusal" model is meaningfully different from PRO's fine mechanism (A2.1 introducing it, sharpened via Q1 in A3.1, contested in B4.1-B4.2, and reasserted decisively in A4.4/A5.1-A5.3) was the pivotal clash, and PRO's framing of it survived CON's closing pushback largely intact.</best_rebuttal>
